title: Four Gates, Four Lessons
subtitle: Cores, the first Gates, and the Gate Evaluation Doctrine
summary: What the first four Gates taught Endros: that taking a Core closes a Gate, that a Gate can be lived in, that surviving a place is not the same as staying in it, and that danger can follow a crew home.
content:
> *"A survivable environment is not necessarily an occupiable environment."*
> — finding of the Gate Evaluation Committee, after Gate Three

Every procedure an Expeditioner meets in Endros, from the clearance forms to the Specimen tags to the question *"did you touch the Core?"*, was learned the hard way at one of the first four Gates. Each taught one lesson, and each lesson cost something: a Gate, a station, a life, or the comfortable belief that the danger stays on the far side of the threshold.

This entry summarises those lessons and the doctrine that grew out of them. Each Gate has its own record: [[white-expanse|G-01, the White Expanse]], [[green-vault|G-02, the Green Vault]], [[red-forest|G-03, the Red Forest]] and [[yellow-mire|G-04, the Yellow Mire]]. For where the Ruins and the settlement got their names, see [[why-we-call-them-the-valeoran-ruins|Why We Call Them the Valeoran Ruins]].

## What a Core Is (and Is Not)

Every confirmed Gate investigated so far has contained, or is believed to contain, an object classified as a **Core**.

Every known Core looks the same: an enormous, nearly perfect white sphere, roughly the size of a small automobile. Its surface is smooth and strongly iridescent, its colour shifting with the angle of view, though no pigment, coating or separate surface layer has ever been found. Around it hangs a luminous phenomenon like an aurora: drifting curtains, bands and arcs of coloured light that extend beyond the sphere itself and behave like neither flame, vapour nor ordinary electrical discharge. Nothing visibly supports it. Observed Cores float.

The name is **historical, not descriptive**. It came into use after Gate One collapsed, and it records a belief: that the sphere is somehow essential to a Gate's stability. What the relationship actually is remains unknown. Only one thing is established:

> **Removing a Core through its Gate causes the Gate to collapse.**

Everything beyond that is theory. One Core has been recovered. It is held in secured storage, and what it is remains one of the open questions of the age.

## Gate One: Discovery

[[white-expanse|Gate One]] was the first confirmed Gate to form among the Valeoran Ruins: a still, frozen plain under a pearl-white sky. Several expeditions into the survey, a crew found a floating white sphere in a basin ringed by mineral spires. Nobody knew what it was. A recovery crew hauled it to the threshold on improvised sledges and portable track.

The moment it crossed, the Gate began to close.

> **From report G-01-17, Core Recovery Incident (excerpt)**
>
> *Witnesses reported immediate movement in the surrounding Valeoran structure. The Gate aperture began contracting within seconds. Personnel remaining beyond the threshold were ordered to abandon all equipment and return immediately. The final expedition member cleared the Gate shortly before aperture failure.*
>
> *No casualties were recorded.*
>
> *Effective immediately, no similar object encountered beyond a Gate is to be moved without explicit authorization.*

That last line is the oldest rule in Gate work. Endros gained a Core and lost a world: the sledges, the instruments, the half-mapped needle fields and the basin itself are on the far side of a door that no longer exists. Whatever is left of Gate One's Resources is all there will ever be.

## Gate Two: Occupation

When a crew found the Core of [[green-vault|Gate Two]], a vast enclosed ecosystem inside what looks like an artificial structure, the lesson of Gate One was fresh. They left it where it was. The University of Verna built a forward laboratory nearby, nicknamed **the Greenhouse**, and people have lived beyond the threshold ever since.

The Gate has stayed stable the whole time. That is the strongest evidence for the working hypothesis that a Gate remains open for as long as its Core remains inside it. It is evidence, not proof, and the Committee's documents are careful to say so.

The Green Vault taught Endros that a Gate can be **a place to work**, not only a place to raid. Two of its Resources are now dependable supplies in the Outpost's workshops. Its maintenance logs are less glamorous: vines in the conduits, fungus in the vents, and a standing instruction not to disturb the Core.

## Gate Three: Escalation

[[red-forest|Gate Three]] looked like the Green Vault's cooler cousin: a dark forest of crimson leaves, manageable wildlife, nothing immediately catastrophic. On the strength of the Vault, a semi-permanent research station was built several kilometres in.

For about four months, **Forward Station Three** worked. Then the attacks grew more frequent, and in the end came from several species at once, at several points on the perimeter, to the sound of continuous Bell-Throat calls. The station was evacuated in the night. Four people were seriously injured. One was never found and is presumed dead.

Whether the forest was *coordinating* is unconfirmed. The Committee's finding did not depend on the answer:

> **Committee finding on the evacuation of Forward Station Three**
>
> *The Green Vault occupation model cannot be assumed applicable to future Gates.*
>
> *A survivable environment is not necessarily an occupiable environment.*

The Gate is still open. Its Core is still inside, about nine kilometres from the threshold. Entry now requires expedition clearance.

## Gate Four: Contamination

[[yellow-mire|Gate Four]] seemed the gentlest of all: a warm amber wetland with no large animals at all. Then the returned equipment began to rot. Metal pitted, rubber cracked, glass clouded. Expeditioners fell ill with fevers and yellow branching marks around small wounds, and then people who had never crossed the threshold fell ill too, because they had handled what came back.

Gate Four became the first Gate classified as a threat to Endros itself. No authorised expedition has entered since, nothing may be taken out, and its Core has never been located.

> **From order G-04-12, Suspension of Operations (excerpt)**
>
> *The following do not constitute proof of safety:*
>
> *absence of symptoms; intact protective clothing; negative surface testing; equipment appearing clean; previous decontamination.*

Quarantine became part of Gate doctrine. So did a new kind of fear: the kind where you cannot tell when you have made the mistake.

## The Gate Evaluation Doctrine

The [Gate Evaluation Committee](outpost.html#gate-evaluation-committee) now approaches every new Gate under ten working assumptions. Expeditioners hear them at their first briefing and, usually, again at their second.

1. A Gate may remain stable indefinitely if its Core remains beyond the threshold.
2. No Core is to be moved without explicit authorization.
3. Initial environmental safety does not imply long-term safety.
4. Permanent structures may alter local conditions.
5. Native life may react differently to repeated human presence.
6. Returned materials may remain hazardous after crossing the threshold.
7. All recovered substances are treated as **Specimens** until properly evaluated.
8. A Specimen becomes a formal **Resource** only after useful anomalous properties are confirmed.
9. Unknown material should not be assumed worthless.
10. Unknown material should also not be assumed safe.

Every one of them can be traced to something that went right, or wrong, at the first four Gates. The last four are also what happens when you put researchers and Expeditioners in the same room for long enough.

> **At the Specimen intake counter, the morning after a return**
>
> The clerk turned the jar under the lamp. Inside, a curl of black bark, still damp.
>
> "Specimen," she said, and wrote out the tag.
>
> "It's Redbark. Everyone knows it's Redbark."
>
> "Everyone knows *Redbark* is Redbark." She tied the tag to the lid. "This is a piece of bark you say came off a Redbark tree. When the laboratory agrees, it can be Redbark too." She slid the jar onto the tray. "Next."

## From Specimen to Resource

Expeditioners may bring back almost anything they can carry: plants, water, stone, soil, shells, bones, fungal growth, residue, abandoned machinery, fragments of built things. All of it enters the record as a **Specimen**. After analysis, a Specimen is filed as one of:

- **Discarded Material**: nothing useful or anomalous identified;
- **Research Specimen**: scientifically interesting, not yet useful;
- **Resource Candidate**: evidence suggests an exploitable anomalous property;
- **Confirmed Resource**: at least one Function identified, and the material entered in the [Resource catalogue](discoveries.html#resources).

Nothing in the first three categories is final. A Glasswing Husk that every new Expeditioner collects and every laboratory ignores could, after the right research, turn out to matter a great deal. The [Research](game.html#post-research) rule covers how hidden properties come to light.

## Before Gate Five

At the time of writing, Endros has **one recovered Core, one closed Gate, one occupied Gate, one hostile Gate and one quarantined Gate**, and no confirmed explanation for what the Gates actually are.

The questions the four Gates raised are argued in every faith and faculty in Endros. Vesperian theologians ask whether taking a Core takes something essential from another world (see [[sacred-flame|The Sacred Flame]]). Kharadi jurists ask whether being able to reach a thing proves you own it (see [[covenant-of-the-one|The Covenant of the One]]). The University asks where each sample came from before it asks what the sample does (see [[university-of-verna|The University of Verna]]). The Committee asks only that nobody moves a Core until those arguments are settled, which may be a long wait.
